tasks.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 736-737); Figure (p. 737); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 737); Discussion, 5th and 7th paragraphs (p. 748); Tables 1 to 4, risk-of-bias column
tasks.extracted: Systematic review of observational studies: MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO from inception to 14 January 2021 with English search terms, plus reference lists; human observational studies comparing higher- with lower-potency cannabis as each study defined it, for depression, anxiety, psychosis or cannabis use disorder; experimental studies, conference abstracts, editorials and correspondence excluded; PROSPERO CRD42021226447. 4,171 titles screened, 89 full texts assessed, 20 articles included, printed as 20 studies with 119,581 participants (8 on psychosis, 8 anxiety, 7 depression, 6 cannabis use disorder); by the editors' count the tables hold 16 distinct studies (the GAP study in four articles, EU-GEI in two), and the printed participant total is smaller than one included survey (181,870). None was rated good on a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (editors' count: 5 fair, 11 poor). No meta-analysis was possible because exposure was self-reported, no precise measure of THC exposure was available and definitions of higher and lower potency differed.

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd, 4th, 7th and 8th paragraphs (pp. 740-742); Table 1 (pp. 738-739)
tasks.extracted: Two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair. UK GAP study (410 patients with first-episode psychosis, 370 controls from the same area): against never-use, skunk-type use adjusted odds ratio 2.91 (95% CI 1.52 to 3.60), hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), daily skunk-type use 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30); onset about 4 years earlier with higher-potency use (hazard ratio 1.68, 1.08 to 2.63). EU-GEI study (901 patients and 1,237 population controls in England, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain and Brazil): types of 10% THC or more against never-use 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5); daily use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6). Both adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco, alcohol and other drugs. UK cohort of 256 patients after a first episode: 58% of those who continued daily use of higher-potency cannabis relapsed within 2 years against 24% of those who had used cannabis in the past (adjusted odds ratio 3.28, 1.22 to 9.18); lower-potency or infrequent higher-potency use 1.82 (0.36 to 8.75); adjusted for alcohol, other illicit drugs, cigarettes, care intensity at onset and medication adherence. None of these three studies looked at concentrates as a separate form.

tasks.locator: Results, 5th, 6th, 9th, 15th and 21st paragraphs (pp. 740-747); Tables 1, 3 and 4 (pp. 739-746)
tasks.extracted: Studies of concentrates, all cross-sectional and rated poor. 20-country online survey of 181,870 (self-report with pictorial aids; adjusted for age, gender, sexual orientation, education and other substance use), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal cannabis: self-reported lifetime psychosis diagnosis 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46), anxiety diagnosis 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01; 1.72, 1.55 to 1.91, against higher-potency herbal), depression diagnosis 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48; 1.15, 1.03 to 1.25, against higher-potency herbal). US sample of 156: concentrate use and psychosis symptoms r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), anxiety 0.21 (-0.10 to 0.49), depression 0.17 (-0.15 to 0.45). US sample of 191, frequent concentrate against frequent herbal use: anxiety means 1.1 and 0.66, depression 0.72 and 0.76, no significant difference. Within-person survey of 574 people who used cannabis in the past year, mostly infrequently: psychosis-like experiences mean 1.1 with concentrates and 1.2 with herbal cannabis (0 to 10 scale; Cohen's d 0.12). 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders, liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis: residual or late-onset psychotic disorder odds ratio 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735), which Table 1 labels no association.

tasks.locator: Results, 14th, 15th, 20th and 21st paragraphs (pp. 746-747); Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 747-748); Tables 3 and 4 (pp. 743-746)
tasks.extracted: Anxiety, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): generalised anxiety disorder more likely with higher-potency use in a UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24 (odds ratio 1.92, 1.11 to 3.32; adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, depression score at 13 and frequency; rated fair); no difference between higher- and lower-potency herbal cannabis in the 20-country survey (1.05, 0.98 to 1.12). Depression, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): a slight increase in the 20-country survey (higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.18, 1.11 to 1.25) and little evidence in the UK sample (1.28, 0.68 to 2.32). Studies of people using medical cannabis (four for anxiety, one rated fair; three for depression, all poor) gave varied results that the authors call hard to interpret. The authors conclude there is some evidence for anxiety and little for depression.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 5th, 6th, 8th and 9th paragraphs (pp. 748-749)
tasks.extracted: Most studies took potency from self-reported product type, an approximate proxy for THC content, and none accounted for THC intake as opposed to content; the authors argue that titration, which evidence suggests is partial, would be expected to weaken rather than inflate associations. Some studies compared higher with lower potency directly and others each with no use, so the contrast can be read only within each study. Cross-sectional designs cannot establish direction: people with poorer mental health might choose higher-potency cannabis as self-medication. There is no agreement on confounders; amount used was adjusted for in only one study; frequency was a covariate in some studies and part of a combined potency-and-frequency variable in others, and may be a confounder or a mediator.

tasks.locator: Contributors; Declaration of interests; Acknowledgments (p. 749); references 14, 15, 22, 27 and 30 (pp. 749-750)
tasks.extracted: Funding: Economic and Social Research Council South West Doctoral Training Partnership studentship (KP); Cancer Research UK Population Researcher Postdoctoral Fellowship C56067/A21330 and project award PPRCPJT\100023 (GT); Wellcome Trust 209158/Z/17/Z (LH); the funder had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing. Interests: GT reports previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and owns a scientific consulting company doing work unrelated to the project; the other authors declare none. The reference list shows the senior author (T P Freeman) as an author of included studies, among them the 2017 butane hash oil survey and the 2019 EU-GEI paper, and L Hines as first author of the 2020 UK sample; no procedure for appraising the authors' own studies is described.

tasks.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 736-737); Results, 1st and 10th paragraphs (pp. 737, 744); Table 2 (pp. 741-742)
tasks.extracted: Systematic review of observational studies (MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO to 14 January 2021; PROSPERO CRD42021226447) comparing higher- with lower-potency cannabis as each study defined it. Six cross-sectional studies examined cannabis use disorder: one rated fair and five poor on a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, for limits in the measure of exposure in all six and in outcome measures, sample selection and confounder adjustment in the poor ones. Exposure was self-reported in all six. Outcomes: Severity of Dependence Scale (two online surveys; 0 to 15, cut-off 3 or more), Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (UK sample of 1,087), MINI cannabis screening test (US sample of 191), a self-report questionnaire (US sample of 156) and an ICD-10 clinical interview (71 Japanese patients).

tasks.locator: Results, 11th paragraph (p. 744); Table 2 (pp. 741-742)
tasks.extracted: UK online survey 2009-10 (2,514; skunk against grass and resin; adjusted for gender and age; poor): each extra day a month of higher-potency use went with a Severity of Dependence Scale score 0.254 higher (95% CI 0.161 to 0.357 in Table 2; 0.161 to 0.3578 in the text), with no association for grass (0.020, -0.029 to 0.070) or resin (0.025, -0.019 to 0.067). Survey of 55,240 people in 175 countries 2017-18 (adjusted for age, gender, amount and frequency of use and tobacco added; poor): the classes using sinsemilla and herbal (b 0.155, 0.100 to 0.209) and hashish and herbal (b 0.262, 0.188 to 0.337) scored higher than the class using herbal only. UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24 (Cannabis Abuse Screening Test; adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, age at first use and frequency; fair): recent cannabis problems with higher-potency use, odds ratio 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81). 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders (ICD-10 interview; no adjustment listed; poor): liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis, dependence syndrome 6.850 (1.866 to 25.145 in Table 2; 6.9, 1.19 to 25.15, in the text).

tasks.locator: Results, 12th and 13th paragraphs (pp. 744-746); Table 2 (p. 741)
tasks.extracted: US sample of 156 people (self-report questionnaire; no adjustment listed; poor): higher-potency herbal use and use-disorder symptoms r 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.30); for concentrates the review prints -0.05 (-0.35 to -0.26), an interval that does not contain its own estimate, and the text reads it as fewer symptoms. US sample of 191 (MINI cannabis screening test; no adjustment listed; poor): people who frequently used concentrates did not endorse significantly more symptoms than people who frequently used herbal cannabis (means 2.1 and 1.3); the review notes that the sample endorsed few symptoms overall. These are the only two studies in the review that compare concentrates with herbal cannabis on cannabis use disorder.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 2nd, 5th, 8th and 11th paragraphs (pp. 747-749)
tasks.extracted: The Discussion states that higher-potency use was consistently associated with an increased risk of cannabis use disorder, recent problems and dependence severity, citing animal self-administration studies and an association of rising potency with treatment entry. The limits it states: self-reported product type as a proxy for THC, THC intake not measured (titration expected to weaken associations), cross-sectional designs that cannot establish direction, no agreement on confounders, and amount used adjusted for in only one study. The Conclusion draws recommendations for education, clinical management and regulation by THC concentration from these findings, without a certainty rating.

tasks.locator: Contributors; Declaration of interests; Acknowledgments (p. 749); references 14, 27 and 30 (pp. 749-750)
tasks.extracted: Funding: ESRC doctoral studentship (KP), Cancer Research UK fellowship and project award (GT), Wellcome Trust (LH); the funder had no role. Interests: GT reports previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and owns a consulting company doing unrelated work; the others declare none. The reference list shows the senior author (T P Freeman) as an author of three of the four cannabis use disorder studies that found an association (the 2015 UK survey, the 2020 175-country survey and the 2020 UK sample, of which review author L Hines is first author); the Japanese study and the two studies that found no clear difference are by other groups.

tasks.locator: Results › Cannabis concentrates › CUD outcomes, paragraph; references 37, 40, 42 and 43 (p. 12)
tasks.extracted: The review states that concentrate use has been consistently associated with a higher cannabis use disorder risk than other forms; that people who frequently use concentrates show more symptoms than people who do not use them but may also use higher-potency cannabis when not using concentrates (ref. 40, Bidwell et al., 2018, the US sample of 191 that the systematic review reports as showing no significant difference); that people who use concentrates chronically may show more tolerance and withdrawal (ref. 37, a 2021 review); that people who regularly use concentrates more often feel worried about their use than people who have tried them (ref. 42, a national web survey of dab use); and that among college students more frequent use of butane hash oil went with more physical symptoms such as tolerance after adjustment for demographic, substance-use and personality covariates (ref. 43). It gives no effect sizes and calls for longitudinal studies.

tasks.locator: Results › Cannabis flower › CUD outcomes, paragraph (p. 6); Discussion › CUD outcomes, paragraph (p. 9)
tasks.extracted: The review calls the literature on problematic use by form small and incomplete and mostly about flower. It cites a positive association between product potency and cannabis use disorder risk (ref. 52), more symptoms with frequent concentrate use than with frequent flower use (ref. 40), more problematic use with more frequent use of the two inhaled forms but not edibles (ref. 39), and more cannabis use disorder with high-frequency use of all three forms than with high-frequency flower-only use (ref. 15); it says, without a citation, that inhaling is generally linked to a higher risk than swallowing. It concludes that frequency of use remains the most reliable predictor of cannabis use disorder risk across all forms and that further causal factors such as quantity and THC potency are yet to be firmly established. For flower, it cites a survey of 617 Colorado college students in which flower potency was positively associated with symptom count and severity (ref. 36), and says flower's outcomes have rarely been compared with other forms.

tasks.locator: Results › Cannabis edibles › CUD outcomes, paragraph; Results › Cannabis edibles › Conclusion, paragraph
tasks.extracted: There is limited information specific to the cannabis use disorder potential of edibles. The review argues from studies of other drugs (refs 50 and 51, formulations of hydrocodone and methylphenidate) that a slower onset of action goes with a lower potential to contribute to a substance use disorder, and cites one source (ref. 44, titled as a study of medical cannabis patients with chronic pain) for people who use cannabis medically preferring oral use and for people new to non-medical use or using it infrequently more often naming edibles as their main form. It concludes that the cannabis use disorder outcomes of edibles have not been sufficiently characterised.

tasks.locator: Abstract and Highlights (p. 3); Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 4-5); Figure 1 (p. 4); Disclosure statement and Funding (p. 10)
tasks.extracted: Narrative review: PubMed keyword searches screened by title and abstract for relevance; 4,077 articles found, 216 reviewed, 20 included and 7 added from reference lists and citing articles, 27 in all; no dates, criteria beyond relevance or appraisal of the included studies are stated; the authors scored their own review 12 of 12 on SANRA. The 72 references do not include the 2022 systematic review (editors' check). The Abstract says concentrate use may be associated with a greater cannabis use disorder risk and that form-specific longitudinal data are lacking; the Highlights state the association without a hedge. No funding; no conflicts reported. Published online 26 October 2024.

tasks.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 2); Results › Meta-analysis results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 11); Table 2 (p. 28)
tasks.extracted: Random-effects pooled shares among people in general-population samples who had used cannabis: cannabis use disorder 22% (95% CI 18 to 26), abuse 13% (8 to 18), dependence 13% (10 to 15). Use disorder by design and recall period: cohorts, lifetime use 27% (25 to 28) and recent use 22% (20 to 24); cross-sectional, lifetime 28% (10 to 48), past year or month 17% (12 to 23), weekly or daily 22% (17 to 28). Dependence: cohorts, lifetime 12% (7 to 18), recent 9% (1 to 19), weekly or daily 33% (22 to 44); cross-sectional, lifetime 11% (7 to 15), recent 8% (6 to 10), daily or near daily 18% (12 to 24). The three pools draw on different sets of studies (255,010, 28,951 and 58,661 observations), so they cannot be added or compared directly.

tasks.locator: Method › Protocol; Selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Search strategy; Analysis, 2nd paragraph (pp. 5-7); Results › Study selection, paragraph; Study characteristics and narrative summary, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 8)
tasks.extracted: PROSPERO CRD42019133166. General-population observational studies with DSM or ICD diagnoses from structured interviews; prisoners and other high-risk or sub-populations excluded; studies published from 2009 (PubMed for cohorts and Global Burden of Disease data sources for surveys, February 2019, updated April 2020). 1,383 records, 130 full texts, 21 studies, 153 data points (several per study, by sex, age, survey year or recall period). Samples from the US, the Netherlands, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and France; 15 studies gave cross-sectional and 9 longitudinal data; 11 sampled adolescents or young adults. Nine counted people who had ever tried cannabis, three required use more than a few times, nine past-year use and four weekly or daily use. One study used DSM-III-R and one DSM-5, the rest DSM-IV, in which use disorder means abuse or dependence; separate analyses by DSM version were planned but are not reported. No appraisal of the included studies is reported.

tasks.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 4th to 6th paragraphs (pp. 9-10); Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 12-13)
tasks.extracted: Single-study estimates: use disorder from 4.5% (1.8 to 7.3) in US adults aged 50 or more who used in the past year (2005-06) to 41.1% (38.4 to 43.8), lifetime, in an Australian cohort of 21-year-olds; abuse from 2.9% to 28.4%; dependence from 3.5% (0.1 to 7.0) in young adults in Ireland to 40.9% (29.0 to 52.8) among people using daily in an Australian adolescent cohort; past-year dependence 14.7% (13.0 to 16.5) among US adults using daily or near daily in 2017. The 33% (22 to 44) for weekly or daily use comes from two longitudinal studies of young people (Australia and the Netherlands); cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use gave 18% (12 to 24). In one US study, dependence was 10.6% (7.1 to 14.1) among everyone who had ever used and 18.1% (12.4 to 23.8) among those who had used more than six times.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 7th to 9th, 11th and 12th paragraphs (pp. 14-16)
tasks.extracted: The authors found no population study that estimated the risk of cannabis use disorder by the potency of the products used, and mention, without a reference, a Michigan study of high-risk families in which people who used higher-potency products had higher risks of developing use-disorder symptoms. Limits they state: heterogeneity, with limited power to detect moderators; 60% of estimates from cross-sectional surveys open to recall bias; lifetime and past-year estimates that differ in meaning (past-year use disorder 15.4% among 18 to 25-year-olds who used that year against 9.8% among those who had ever used, in one US survey); all studies from high-income countries, over half from the US.

tasks.locator: Role of Funding Sources; Contributors; Conflict of Interest
tasks.extracted: University of Queensland development fellowship (JL); NHMRC Senior Research Fellowship (LH); the authors' centre and group (Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research; Lives Lived Well) supported by Australian Government Drug and Alcohol Program funding; the funding bodies had no role.
